name: Titanium dioxide
lead: Titanium dioxide (TiO2), also called titanium white or CI 77891, is a white, water-insoluble mineral compound and the most widely used white pigment. It is found in paints, plastics, paper and toothpaste as well as cosmetics [1]. In skincare it serves as a mineral (physical) UV filter and as a pigment in tinted products. For appearance, the practical benefit is daily sun protection that helps limit sunburn, tanning, uneven pigmentation and photoageing, together with a tint or soft-focus finish when the pigment is used in makeup [10].

In sunscreen it is usually paired with zinc oxide. Wikipedia describes mineral filters as working mainly by absorbing UV, with some reflection and scattering, and notes that titanium dioxide gives good protection but does not fully cover the UVA range; zinc oxide has been reported to be superior at 340 to 380 nm [2]. Since 2019 the FDA has sorted UV filters into categories, and as of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were recognised as generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE) [2].

Safety discussion centres on nanoparticle forms and on inhalation. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies inhaled titanium dioxide dust as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans, and advises against sprayable sunscreens because of inhalation risk [1]. The EU withdrew authorisation of E171 as a food additive in 2022 after the European Food Safety Authority could not rule out genotoxicity; this does not concern its use in sunscreen [1][3].

Mineral sunscreens and tinted SPF with titanium dioxide are discussed in skincare communities as options for sensitive skin and for people who prefer non-chemical filters, set against the white cast that larger particles can leave.[2][9]

paras: Titanium dioxide occurs naturally as the minerals rutile, anatase and brookite, and cosmetic grades are manufactured to high purity and often coated with alumina, silica or other materials to improve dispersion [3]. Its very high refractive index is what makes it opaque and bright white, and the same property lets it scatter visible light [3]. In cosmetics the pigment appears on ingredient lists as CI 77891 [1].

Two particle-size regimes matter in skincare. Pigment-grade particles are larger and opaque, which suits foundations and tinted products. Nanoparticle grades, below about 100 nm, are used in sunscreens so that the film looks sheer rather than chalky [10][9]. A JAAD review notes that because nano mineral filters are nearly invisible, they do not by themselves protect against visible light, whereas tinted sunscreens that combine iron oxides with pigmentary titanium dioxide do [9].

Titanium dioxide was first mass-produced as a pigment in 1916 and became the most widely used white pigment, found in paints, plastics, paper and toothpaste.[1] Akira Fujishima discovered its photocatalytic behaviour in 1967 and published in 1972, an effect now called the Honda-Fujishima effect, and his group reported superhydrophilicity on coated glass in 1995, leading to self-cleaning glass.[1]

In sunscreen history, Franz Greiter's sun protection factor became the global standard for UVB protection in 1974, adapting earlier calculations by Friedrich Ellinger and Rudolf Schulze.[2] The nanoparticle grades used in sunscreens were developed to avoid white residue, though public concern has slowed their acceptance, according to a 2021 review that argues regulation is strict and gaps in knowledge sustain the worry.[15]

Titanium dioxide is used in sunscreens, foundations, powders and tinted SPF, typically as a pigment at low single-digit percentages in colour cosmetics [3]. Nano-sized particles give a sheerer finish, and cited studies report higher SPF than equal concentrations of larger particles [3]. Mineral sunscreens made with larger particles can leave an opaque white cast that consumers often reject, and people may apply them less thickly, which reduces effective protection [2]. Adding iron oxide or pigmentary titanium dioxide has been reported to improve visible-light protection [2].

Beyond skincare, it is used as a food whitener (E171), in toothpaste and in paints, which consume roughly half of world production [1][3]. Its photocatalytic properties, discovered by Akira Fujishima, underpin self-cleaning and anti-fogging coatings and solar-cell research [1][4][5].

The compound scatters and reflects light and absorbs UV. Anatase is more photoactive than rutile: under UV light it generates hydroxyl radicals [3]. Coatings of alumina or silica are used on cosmetic and paint grades to improve dispersion and weather resistance [3].

Wikipedia notes that mineral filters work mainly by absorbing UV, with some reflection and scattering, a point it attributes to a 2015 analysis arguing absorption is the main mechanism.[2] Manufacturing uses either the chloride process or the sulfate process from ilmenite and other ores, and about 9.9 million tonnes of pigment capacity existed in 2025, with China accounting for 6.0 million.[1]

Reviews of inorganic filters describe zinc oxide as having a broad UVA-UVB absorption curve and titanium dioxide as providing comparatively better UVB protection, which is why the two are often combined in one product [10]. A 2008 review comparing organic and inorganic filters covered their absorption properties, photostability and the role of sunscreen in melanoma prevention [11].

Authors of a 2019 dermatology review reported that the human health risk from inorganic filters is very low because of the lack of percutaneous absorption, while noting potential concerns where inhalation can occur, such as sprays and powders [10]. A review in the European dermatology literature found that most human and animal studies showed nano titanium dioxide did not pass beyond the outer layers of the stratum corneum to viable cells or reach general circulation, in healthy or compromised skin [8].

Wikipedia reports that titanium dioxide gives good protection but does not fully cover the UVA range, with early-2000s research finding zinc oxide superior at 340 to 380 nm.[2] Mineral formulas can leave a visible white cast that makes people reluctant to apply them thickly enough, and some studies suggest large-particle formulas or ones with iron oxide or pigmentary titanium dioxide offer some visible-light protection.[2][9] FDA consumer guidance describes broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher, reapplication at least every two hours, and about one ounce for the body as general sun-safety practice.[13]

In the US, FDA regulates sunscreens as nonprescription drugs. In February 2019 it began sorting filters into generally recognised as safe and effective (GRASE), non-GRASE and needing further data, and as of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were recognised as GRASE; PABA and trolamine salicylate were removed that year.[2][13] FDA noted that some active ingredients are absorbed through the skin and requested industry data.[13] US labels need not disclose nanoparticle content whereas EU labels must.[2]

For food, the US FDA approved titanium dioxide as a colour additive in 1966 with a cap of 1% of a food's weight.[1] France banned it in food from 2020. On 6 May 2021 the European Food Safety Authority concluded E171 could no longer be considered safe as a food additive because genotoxicity could not be ruled out and no acceptable daily intake could be set; EFSA noted up to 50% of E171 particles may be in the nano range, and said its opinion did not cover cosmetics, paints or medicines.[12] The EU removed authorisation effective 7 February 2022, while the UK and Canada did not follow.[1] Industry responses included Dunkin' Donuts dropping it from merchandise in 2015 and Mars removing it from Skittles in 2025.[1]

Non-nano particles stay largely in the outer skin layer, and Grokipedia, citing studies, reports about 5% reaching the upper epidermis and about 0.1% the dermis with no significant systemic absorption after repeated use; that page itself contains uncited statements [3]. A 2012 study examined titanium dioxide nanoparticles in food and personal care products as sources of environmental release [6]. A 2015 study found titanium dioxide nanoparticles under UV light increased hydrogen peroxide, which can damage phytoplankton, and environmental advocates often recommend mineral sunscreens for reef protection as a precaution [2]. About 99% of nanoparticles reaching wastewater end up in sewage sludge [1].

IARC (2010) classified titanium dioxide Group 2B largely on high-dose rat inhalation data; Grokipedia argues human worker cohorts show no consistent excess of lung cancer [3]. In 2025 the Court of Justice of the EU upheld the annulment of the CLP classification of certain titanium dioxide powders as an inhalation carcinogen, with the food ban unaffected [3].

A 2015 review of dermal absorption of metal-oxide nanoparticles from sunscreens found most studies show particles stay on the skin surface, while noting that study variables affect measured penetration and proposing a research agenda for remaining uncertainty.[17] A decade of in vivo multiphoton microscopy studies on human skin reported that nanoparticulate zinc oxide does not penetrate under various application conditions.[16] A 2025 JAAD review of sunscreen regulation and safety found organic filters are absorbed systemically without clear evidence of harm and discussed questions about vitamin D, benzene contamination and coral bleaching.[14] A 2023 review covers properties, toxicity and regulation of inorganic nanoparticles in cosmetics.[18] NIOSH recommends exposure limits of 2.4 mg/m3 for fine and 0.3 mg/m3 for ultrafine dust, which concern workers.[1] FDA notes that spray sunscreens should not be sprayed directly on the face and can be flammable.[13]

A registered phase 4 study (NCT01021787, started 2009, n=26) examined dermal penetration of titanium dioxide from an SPF40 sunscreen cream in volunteers [7]. Other registered trials involving titanium dioxide are dental or environmental and unrelated to skin appearance.

Most of the human-relevant literature consists of reviews. The 2019 JEADV review of nanoparticles in cosmetics summarised human and animal penetration studies and the opinions of European scientific committees on consumer safety [8]. The Photodermatology review covers use in preventing keratinocyte cancer and photoageing and compares the filters with organic ones that have been questioned on environmental grounds [10]. The JAAD tinted-sunscreen review discusses visible-light-induced erythema and pigmentation, with tinted products offering protection that clear mineral filters do not [9].

Mineral sunscreens and tinted SPF containing titanium dioxide are discussed in skincare communities as options for sensitive skin or for avoiding organic filters, set against concerns over white cast. These are general sunscreen discussions rather than claims specific to the compound. Tinted mineral products are also promoted to people with darker skin because visible light can trigger pigmentation in dark-skinned individuals.[9] Mineral filters are marketed as an alternative to oxybenzone and octinoxate, which Hawaii banned in 2018 and 2021; 'reef-safe' labels are unregulated.[2][10]

Titanium dioxide enters the environment mainly as nanoparticles through wastewater treatment, and about 99% of them end up in sewage sludge.[1] A 2012 study examined nanoparticles in food and personal care products as sources of release, and a 2015 study found particles under UV light increased hydrogen peroxide that can damage phytoplankton.[6][2] Environmental advocates often recommend mineral sunscreens for reefs as a precaution.[2]

lore.intro: Titanium dioxide comes up in skincare discussion through mineral-versus-chemical sunscreen debates, white cast, nanoparticle concerns and reef-safe marketing; the claims below are those described in published reviews and encyclopedias rather than from a single forum.[2][10]

claims.claim: Mineral sunscreens are safer than chemical ones
claims.believers: Advocates prefer mineral filters because titanium dioxide and zinc oxide largely stay on the skin surface and are less associated with systemic absorption.[10][17]
claims.experts: A 2019 review reports very low human health risk from inorganic filters because of lack of percutaneous absorption, and a 2025 JAAD review found organic filters absorbed systemically without clear evidence of harm.[10][14]

claims.claim: Titanium dioxide gives full broad-spectrum protection
claims.believers: Products pairing it with zinc oxide are marketed as broad-spectrum mineral protection.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports it covers UVB and UVA II well but not the full UVA range, which is why it is usually paired with zinc oxide.[2][10]

claims.claim: Nano titanium dioxide passes through skin into the body
claims.believers: Some consumers avoid nano sunscreens because of fears about particle penetration.[15]
claims.experts: A European review found most studies show nano titanium dioxide does not pass beyond the outer layers of the stratum corneum, in healthy or compromised skin.[8][17]

claims.believers: Advocates cite IARC's Group 2B classification and the EU food ban.[1]
claims.experts: The classification concerns inhaled dust and led IARC to advise against sprayable sunscreens, and EFSA's opinion did not cover cosmetics.[1][12]

claims.believers: Environmental advocates recommend mineral filters as a precaution for coral reefs.[2]
claims.experts: Studies found nanoparticles under UV light increased hydrogen peroxide that can damage phytoplankton, and 'reef-safe' labels are unregulated.[2]

claims.claim: Tinted mineral sunscreen protects against visible light pigmentation
claims.believers: Products with iron oxide and pigmentary titanium dioxide are promoted to people with darker skin.[9]
claims.experts: A JAAD review notes nano mineral filters are nearly invisible and do not protect against visible light, while tinted sunscreens with iron oxide and pigmentary titanium dioxide do.[9]

claims.claim: White cast makes mineral sunscreens impractical
claims.believers: Consumers often reject chalky formulas or apply thinly.[2]
claims.experts: Nano grades were developed to avoid white residue, and thin application reduces effective protection.[15][2]

card.summary: The classic mineral UV filter and white pigment in physical sunscreens and tinted SPF; broad but weaker on UVA I.
card.note: Inhalation concerns (IARC 2B) apply to dust and sprays; EU banned E171 in food, not in sunscreen.

quick.overview:
Titanium dioxide is a white mineral used as a physical sunscreen filter and a pigment in tinted SPF. Together with zinc oxide it was the only filter the FDA recognised as GRASE as of 2021.

It gives good UVB and UVA II coverage but is weaker in UVA I, and larger particles can leave a white cast.
quick.mechanism: It scatters and reflects light and absorbs UV. Nano-sized particles give a sheerer finish.
quick.risks: IARC classes inhaled dust as Group 2B and advises against sprayable sunscreens. The EU removed it as a food additive in 2022. Non-nano particles mostly stay in the outer skin layer, though nanoparticle effects on aquatic life are studied.

chain: Titanium dioxide scatters, reflects and absorbs UV
Less sunburn, tanning and pigmentation from sun
Even tone and slower photoageing; tint or soft-focus finish in makeup
angle.text: Titanium dioxide in sunscreen and tinted SPF is a daily-wear UV barrier, and the same pigment gives foundations and powders their opacity and brightness.[10][3] Sun protection is how people use it to protect complexion and limit uneven pigmentation and photoageing.
